Explain the cause, how you would confirm it, and two ways to fix it. *Hint:* Paige: orthogonality is lost exactly as Ritz values converge; check $\lVert Q_k^TQ_k - I \rVert$; fix with full or selective reorthogonalization (using modified Gram-Schmidt or a second pass), or switch to an implicitly restarted library routine such as ARPACK's `eigsh`.

<a id="13-advanced-topics-and-applications"></a>
## 13. Advanced Topics and Applications

The previous chapters built a complete theory of vectors, linear maps, eigenvalues, and their computation. This chapter shows how far that theory reaches. It covers multilinear algebra (forms, tensors, wedge and Kronecker products), the spectral theory of nonnegative matrices and graphs, six applied domains where linear algebra does most of the work, and the branches of mathematics that start where a first course ends. The goal is to recognize the same few ideas (bases, eigenvectors, orthogonality, factorizations) in settings that look different at first.

<a id="131-multilinear-algebra"></a>
### 13.1 Multilinear Algebra

Linear algebra studies functions that are linear in one vector argument. Multilinear algebra studies functions that are linear in each of several arguments separately (inner products, determinants, stress tensors), and the vector spaces built to turn them back into ordinary linear maps.

#### Bilinear and Sesquilinear Forms

**Why it matters.** Many core objects in this guide take two vectors and return a scalar: the dot product (Section 2.3), general inner products (Section 9.1), and the quadratic forms $\mathbf{x}^TA\mathbf{x}$ of Section 10.2. Each is linear in each argument when the other is held fixed. Studying this property on its own, without assuming symmetry or positivity, gives a single framework for all of them. It also covers forms that are not inner products at all, such as the Minkowski form of special relativity and the symplectic form of classical mechanics.

**Analogy.** A linear functional is a machine with one input slot that turns a vector into a number. A bilinear form is a machine with two slots. Freeze either input, and what remains is an ordinary linear functional of the other.

**Definition.** Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$. A **bilinear form** is a map $B : V \times V \to F$ such that, for all vectors and scalars,

$$B(a\mathbf{u} + b\mathbf{v}, \mathbf{w}) = aB(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{w}) + bB(\mathbf{v}, \mathbf{w}), \qquad B(\mathbf{u}, a\mathbf{v} + b\mathbf{w}) = aB(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}) + bB(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{w}).$$

**Matrix representation.** Fix a basis $\mathbf{e}_1, \dots, \mathbf{e}_n$ and set $A_{ij} = B(\mathbf{e}_i, \mathbf{e}_j)$. Bilinearity then gives, for coordinate vectors $\mathbf{x}$ and $\mathbf{y}$,

$$B(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}) = \sum_{i,j} x_iy_jB(\mathbf{e}_i, \mathbf{e}_j) = \mathbf{x}^TA\mathbf{y}.$$

So bilinear forms on $F^n$ correspond one to one with $n \times n$ matrices. The matrix, however, depends on the basis, and it transforms differently from the matrix of a linear operator. If the new basis vectors are the columns of an invertible $P$, then $\mathbf{x} = P\mathbf{x}'$ and

$$B(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}) = (P\mathbf{x}')^TA(P\mathbf{y}') = \mathbf{x}'^T(P^TAP)\mathbf{y}'.$$

| | Linear operator $T : V \to V$ | Bilinear form $B : V \times V \to F$ |
|---|---|---|
| Matrix entry | $A_{ij}$ = $i$-th coordinate of $T\mathbf{e}_j$ | $A_{ij} = B(\mathbf{e}_i, \mathbf{e}_j)$ |
| Change of basis | similarity $P^{-1}AP$ | congruence $P^TAP$ |
| Invariants | eigenvalues, trace, determinant | rank, signature (for symmetric forms); $\det$ only up to a factor $\det(P)^2$ |
| Canonical form | Jordan form (Section 8.3) | $\operatorname{diag}(1, \dots, 1, -1, \dots, -1, 0, \dots, 0)$ over $\mathbb{R}$ (Section 10.2) |

When $P$ is orthogonal, $P^T = P^{-1}$ and the two transformations coincide. This is why symmetric matrices can be studied with either point of view.

**Symmetry types.** A form is **symmetric** if $B(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}) = B(\mathbf{v}, \mathbf{u})$ (matrix $A = A^T$) and **skew-symmetric** if $B(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}) = -B(\mathbf{v}, \mathbf{u})$ ($A = -A^T$). Away from characteristic 2, every form splits uniquely as the sum of the two: $A = \tfrac12(A + A^T) + \tfrac12(A - A^T)$. A skew-symmetric form satisfies $B(\mathbf{v}, \mathbf{v}) = 0$ for every $\mathbf{v}$, so the quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x}) = B(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x})$ only sees the symmetric part. The symmetric form can be recovered from $Q$ by the **polarization identity**:

$$B(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}) = \tfrac12\big(Q(\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}) - Q(\mathbf{u}) - Q(\mathbf{v})\big).$$

**Nondegeneracy.** The **radical** of a symmetric form is $\{\mathbf{u} : B(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}) = 0 \text{ for all } \mathbf{v}\}$, which is the null space of $A$. The form is **nondegenerate** when the radical is $\{\mathbf{0}\}$, that is, when $A$ is invertible. A nondegenerate form identifies $V$ with its dual $V^*$ (Section 7.4), by sending $\mathbf{u}$ to the functional $B(\mathbf{u}, \cdot)$. Nondegenerate does not mean positive definite:

| Form on $\mathbb{R}^n$ | Matrix | Nondegenerate? | Positive definite? | Where it appears |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Dot product | $I_n$ | yes | yes | Euclidean geometry |
| Minkowski form | $\operatorname{diag}(-1, 1, 1, 1)$ | yes | no (signature $(3, 1)$) | special relativity |
| Symplectic form | $\begin{bmatrix} 0 & I \\ -I & 0 \end{bmatrix}$ | yes | no (skew) | Hamiltonian mechanics |
| $Q(x, y) = x^2$ | $\operatorname{diag}(1, 0)$ | no (radical = $y$-axis) | no | degenerate conics |

**Sesquilinear forms.** Over $\mathbb{C}$, bilinearity is the wrong requirement for a length. If $B$ were bilinear, then $B(i\mathbf{v}, i\mathbf{v}) = i^2B(\mathbf{v}, \mathbf{v}) = -B(\mathbf{v}, \mathbf{v})$, so no nonzero vector could have positive "squared length" for both $\mathbf{v}$ and $i\mathbf{v}$. The fix is to conjugate scalars in one slot. A **sesquilinear form** ("one and a half linear") is conjugate-linear in the first argument and linear in the second:

$$h(a\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}) = \bar{a}\,h(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}), \qquad h(\mathbf{u}, a\mathbf{v}) = a\,h(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}).$$

Its matrix form is $h(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}) = \mathbf{x}^*H\mathbf{y}$, and a change of basis gives $P^*HP$. The form is **Hermitian** when $h(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}) = \overline{h(\mathbf{v}, \mathbf{u})}$, equivalently $H = H^*$. Then $h(\mathbf{v}, \mathbf{v})$ is always real, so positivity makes sense. A positive definite Hermitian form is exactly a complex inner product (Section 9.1).

*Convention warning.* Physics and most numerical libraries make the first slot conjugate-linear, as here (`np.vdot` conjugates its first argument). Many mathematics texts conjugate the second slot instead. The theory is identical; only the bookkeeping changes.

```python
import numpy as np

# A bilinear form on R^2 given by a formula, and its matrix A_ij = B(e_i, e_j)
def B(x, y):
    return 2*x[0]*y[0] + 3*x[0]*y[1] - x[1]*y[0] + 4*x[1]*y[1]

E = np.eye(2)
A = np.array([[B(E[i], E[j]) for j in range(2)] for i in range(2)])
print(A)                                      # [[ 2.  3.] [-1.  4.]]
x, y = np.array([1.0, 2.0]), np.array([-3.0, 1.0])
print(B(x, y), x @ A @ y)                     # 11.0 11.0

# Split into symmetric and skew-symmetric parts
S, K = (A + A.T) / 2, (A - A.T) / 2
print(S, K, sep="\n")                         # [[2. 1.] [1. 4.]]  and  [[ 0.  2.] [-2.  0.]]
print(x @ K @ x)                              # 0.0: a skew form vanishes on the diagonal

# Congruence P^T S P preserves the signature (Sylvester), not the eigenvalues
M = np.array([[1.0, 2.0, 0.0], [2.0, -3.0, 1.0], [0.0, 1.0, 0.5]])
P = np.array([[1.0, 4.0, -2.0], [0.0, 1.0, 3.0], [2.0, 0.0, 1.0]])   # any invertible P
M2 = P.T @ M @ P
for X in (M, M2):
    ev = np.linalg.eigvalsh(X)
    print(np.round(ev, 3), (ev > 0).sum(), (ev < 0).sum())
# [-4.018  0.577  1.942] 2 1
# [-43.182   2.744  31.938] 2 1    different eigenvalues, same inertia (2 positive, 1 negative)

# A Hermitian sesquilinear form h(x, y) = x^* H y takes real values on the diagonal
H = np.array([[2.0, 1 - 1j], [1 + 1j, 3.0]])
z = np.array([1 + 2j, -1j])
w = np.array([0.5, 2 - 1j])
h = lambda x, y: np.conj(x) @ H @ y
print(h(z, z))                                # (7+0j): real
print(np.isclose(h(z, w), np.conj(h(w, z))))  # True: conjugate symmetry
print(np.isclose(h(1j * z, z), -1j * h(z, z)))   # True: conjugate-linear in the first slot
```

**Key takeaways**

- A bilinear form is linear in each argument separately; in a basis it is $\mathbf{x}^TA\mathbf{y}$ with $A_{ij} = B(\mathbf{e}_i, \mathbf{e}_j)$.
- Form matrices change by congruence $P^TAP$, not by similarity; eigenvalues are not invariant, but rank and signature are (Sylvester's law).
- Every form is the sum of a symmetric part (which determines the quadratic form) and a skew-symmetric part (which vanishes on the diagonal).
- Nondegenerate means $A$ is invertible, which is weaker than positive definite: the Minkowski and symplectic forms are nondegenerate but not definite.
- Over $\mathbb{C}$, use sesquilinear forms $\mathbf{x}^*H\mathbf{y}$; Hermitian ones take real values on the diagonal, and positive definite Hermitian forms are complex inner products.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. Find the matrix of $B(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}) = x_1y_2 - x_2y_1 + 3x_3y_3$ on $\mathbb{R}^3$. Split it into symmetric and skew-symmetric parts and decide whether $B$ is nondegenerate.
> 2. Show that $B(f, g) = \int_0^1 f(t)g(t)\,dt + f(0)g(1)$ is a bilinear form on polynomials of degree at most 1. Compute its matrix in the basis $\{1, t\}$. Is it symmetric?
> 3. Prove that $\det(P^TAP) = \det(P)^2\det(A)$, and conclude that over $\mathbb{R}$ the *sign* of the determinant of a symmetric form is basis independent.
> 4. **Interview:** Why does a complex inner product need a conjugate in one argument, and what goes wrong if you implement $\langle \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \rangle$ as `x @ y` for complex arrays? *Hint:* evaluate $\langle \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x} \rangle$ for $\mathbf{x} = (1, i)$, then compare with `np.vdot`.

#### Tensor Products of Vector Spaces

**Why it matters.** Bilinear maps are not linear maps, so none of the earlier machinery (kernels, matrices, rank) applies to them directly. The tensor product $V \otimes W$ is a new vector space built so that every bilinear map out of $V \times W$ becomes an ordinary linear map out of $V \otimes W$. The same construction describes composite quantum systems (Section 13.3), multi-index arrays in data science, and the Kronecker products used in numerical linear algebra.

**Analogy.** A recipe combines an amount of flour with an amount of sugar. The direct sum $V \oplus W$ keeps the two lists side by side: $m + n$ numbers. The tensor product records every pairwise interaction, like a multiplication table: $mn$ numbers, one for each pair of basis vectors.

**The defining (universal) property.** The tensor product of $V$ and $W$ is a vector space $V \otimes W$ together with a bilinear map $(\mathbf{v}, \mathbf{w}) \mapsto \mathbf{v} \otimes \mathbf{w}$ such that every bilinear map $\beta : V \times W \to U$ factors uniquely through a linear map $L$:

```text
        V x W ----- (v, w) |-> v (x) w ----->  V (x) W
             \                                   |
              \  beta (bilinear)                 |  L (linear, unique)
               \                                 v
                `------------------------------> U

        beta(v, w) = L(v (x) w)   for all v, w
```

**Concrete construction.** If $\mathbf{e}_1, \dots, \mathbf{e}_m$ is a basis of $V$ and $\mathbf{f}_1, \dots, \mathbf{f}_n$ a basis of $W$, then the $mn$ symbols $\mathbf{e}_i \otimes \mathbf{f}_j$ form a basis of $V \otimes W$, so

$$\dim(V \otimes W) = \dim V \cdot \dim W.$$

The product of two vectors expands by bilinearity: $\mathbf{v} \otimes \mathbf{w} = \sum_{i,j} v_iw_j\,(\mathbf{e}_i \otimes \mathbf{f}_j)$. Its coordinates $v_iw_j$ form the $m \times n$ matrix $\mathbf{v}\mathbf{w}^T$. This identifies $F^m \otimes F^n$ with the space of $m \times n$ matrices, with pure tensors $\mathbf{v} \otimes \mathbf{w}$ corresponding to outer products.

**Computation rules.** These follow from bilinearity:

- $(\mathbf{v}_1 + \mathbf{v}_2) \otimes \mathbf{w} = \mathbf{v}_1 \otimes \mathbf{w} + \mathbf{v}_2 \otimes \mathbf{w}$, and likewise in the second slot.
- $(a\mathbf{v}) \otimes \mathbf{w} = \mathbf{v} \otimes (a\mathbf{w}) = a(\mathbf{v} \otimes \mathbf{w})$. Scalars move freely between factors.
- $\mathbf{0} \otimes \mathbf{w} = \mathbf{v} \otimes \mathbf{0} = \mathbf{0}$.
- $\mathbf{v} \otimes \mathbf{w} \ne \mathbf{w} \otimes \mathbf{v}$ in general. When $V = W$, they are different elements of $V \otimes V$.

**Pure tensors versus general tensors.** An element of the form $\mathbf{v} \otimes \mathbf{w}$ is called **pure** (or simple, or decomposable). Most elements of $V \otimes W$ are *not* pure; they are sums of pure tensors. Under the matrix identification, pure tensors are exactly the rank-1 matrices, and the smallest number of pure tensors needed to write $T$ is the rank of the matrix $T$. The SVD (Section 11.1) writes any $T$ as a sum of $\operatorname{rank}(T)$ pure tensors $\sigma_k\mathbf{u}_k \otimes \mathbf{v}_k$. In quantum mechanics, non-pure tensors are called **entangled** states.

| | Direct sum $V \oplus W$ | Tensor product $V \otimes W$ |
|---|---|---|
| Elements | pairs $(\mathbf{v}, \mathbf{w})$ | sums $\sum_k \mathbf{v}_k \otimes \mathbf{w}_k$ |
| Dimension | $m + n$ | $mn$ |
| Basis | $\{(\mathbf{e}_i, \mathbf{0})\} \cup \{(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{f}_j)\}$ | $\{\mathbf{e}_i \otimes \mathbf{f}_j\}$ |
| Scaling | $a(\mathbf{v}, \mathbf{w}) = (a\mathbf{v}, a\mathbf{w})$ | $a(\mathbf{v} \otimes \mathbf{w}) = (a\mathbf{v}) \otimes \mathbf{w}$ |
| Linearizes | pairs of linear maps | bilinear maps |
| Physics | independent systems with additive degrees of freedom | composite quantum systems |

**Tensor products of maps.** Linear maps $S : V \to V'$ and $R : W \to W'$ induce a linear map $S \otimes R : V \otimes W \to V' \otimes W'$, defined on pure tensors by $(S \otimes R)(\mathbf{v} \otimes \mathbf{w}) = S\mathbf{v} \otimes R\mathbf{w}$. In coordinates, its matrix is the Kronecker product of the two matrices (last topic of this subchapter). Two standard isomorphisms connect tensor products to earlier chapters:

$$\mathcal{L}(V, W) \cong V^* \otimes W, \qquad \{\text{bilinear forms on } V \times W\} \cong (V \otimes W)^* \cong V^* \otimes W^*.$$

The first says that a rank-1 linear map $\mathbf{x} \mapsto \varphi(\mathbf{x})\,\mathbf{w}$ is the pure tensor $\varphi \otimes \mathbf{w}$, so a general matrix is a sum of such maps.

```python
import numpy as np

v = np.array([1.0, 2.0])                      # v in V = R^2
w = np.array([3.0, 0.0, -1.0])                # w in W = R^3

# v (x) w  <->  the 2x3 matrix v w^T, coordinates in the basis e_i (x) f_j
T = np.outer(v, w)
print(T)                                      # [[ 3.  0. -1.] [ 6.  0. -2.]]
print(np.linalg.matrix_rank(T))               # 1: pure tensors are exactly the rank-1 matrices

# A general tensor is a sum of pure tensors; its tensor rank is the matrix rank
U = np.outer([1, 0], [1, 0, 0]) + np.outer([0, 1], [0, 1, 0])   # e1(x)f1 + e2(x)f2
print(np.linalg.matrix_rank(U))               # 2: not of the form v (x) w for any v, w

# Bilinearity: (2v) (x) w = v (x) (2w) = 2 (v (x) w)
print(np.allclose(np.outer(2 * v, w), np.outer(v, 2 * w)))   # True

# Universal property: the bilinear map beta(v, w) = v^T A w factors through v (x) w
# as the LINEAR functional  L(T) = sum_ij A_ij T_ij  (the Frobenius inner product <A, T>)
A = np.array([[1.0, -2.0, 0.5], [4.0, 0.0, 3.0]])
beta = v @ A @ w
L = lambda T: np.sum(A * T)                   # linear in T
print(beta, L(np.outer(v, w)))                # 2.5 2.5

# Linear maps act factor-wise: (S (x) R)(v (x) w) = Sv (x) Rw
S = np.array([[0.0, 1.0], [1.0, 1.0]])
R = np.array([[2.0, 0.0, 0.0], [0.0, 1.0, 1.0], [1.0, 0.0, 1.0]])
lhs = np.kron(S, R) @ np.kron(v, w)           # Kronecker product = matrix of S (x) R
rhs = np.kron(S @ v, R @ w)
print(np.allclose(lhs, rhs))                  # True
```

**Key takeaways**

- $V \otimes W$ is the space that turns bilinear maps out of $V \times W$ into linear maps; this universal property defines it up to isomorphism.
- A basis is $\{\mathbf{e}_i \otimes \mathbf{f}_j\}$, so dimensions multiply, unlike direct sums, where they add.
- $F^m \otimes F^n$ is the space of $m \times n$ matrices, with $\mathbf{v} \otimes \mathbf{w} = \mathbf{v}\mathbf{w}^T$; pure tensors are rank-1 matrices, and most tensors are not pure.
- $S \otimes R$ acts factor by factor, and its matrix is the Kronecker product.

> 2. Decide whether $\mathbf{e}_1 \otimes \mathbf{e}_1 + \mathbf{e}_1 \otimes \mathbf{e}_2 + \mathbf{e}_2 \otimes \mathbf{e}_1 + \mathbf{e}_2 \otimes \mathbf{e}_2$ is a pure tensor. If it is, find $\mathbf{v}$ and $\mathbf{w}$ with $T = \mathbf{v} \otimes \mathbf{w}$.
> 3. Let $P_2$ be the polynomials of degree at most 2. Show that $P_2 \otimes P_2$ is isomorphic to the space of polynomials $p(x, y)$ of degree at most 2 in each variable, via $p \otimes q \mapsto p(x)q(y)$. What is its dimension?

Stored densely as a tensor in $\mathbb{R}^{10^3} \otimes \mathbb{R}^{10^3} \otimes \mathbb{R}^{10^2}$ it has $10^8$ entries. How would you store and compute with it if you believe it is approximately low rank? *Hint:* sums of $r$ pure tensors need $r(m + n + p)$ numbers (a CP decomposition); compare with $mnp$.

#### Tensors and Index Notation

**Why it matters.** Physics and engineering describe quantities that need more than one index: the stress inside a material, the curvature of spacetime, the elasticity that links strain to stress. The question that matters is how their components change when the coordinate system changes, because physical laws must not depend on that choice. Index notation, with the Einstein summation convention, makes this bookkeeping almost mechanical, and it is exactly what `np.einsum` implements.

**Analogy.** A tensor is like a sentence and its components are a translation. Changing basis is changing language: the words (components) all change, but by fixed rules, so the meaning (the tensor itself) is the same.

**Tensors of type $(p, q)$.** A **tensor of type $(p, q)$** on $V$ is an element of

$$\underbrace{V \otimes \cdots \otimes V}_{p} \otimes \underbrace{V^* \otimes \cdots \otimes V^*}_{q},$$

or equivalently a multilinear map that eats $q$ vectors and $p$ covectors (linear functionals) and returns a scalar. Its **order** is $p + q$, the number of indices. Common examples:

| Type | Example | Components | Order |
|---|---|---|---|
| $(0, 0)$ | scalar (temperature) | $s$ | 0 |
| $(1, 0)$ | vector (velocity) | $v^i$ | 1 |
| $(0, 1)$ | covector (gradient $df$, linear functional) | $a_i$ | 1 |
| $(1, 1)$ | linear operator $V \to V$ | $A^i{}_j$ | 2 |
| $(0, 2)$ | bilinear form, metric tensor | $g_{ij}$ | 2 |
| $(1, 3)$ | Riemann curvature tensor | $R^i{}_{jkl}$ | 4 |

*Terminology clash.* In machine learning, "tensor" usually just means a multidimensional array, with no transformation rule attached, and "rank" often means the number of axes. In multilinear algebra, "rank" means the minimum number of pure tensors in a decomposition (previous topic). This guide uses **order** for the number of indices.

**Upper and lower indices.** Vector components carry upper indices and covector components carry lower ones. The placement records how the components respond to a change of basis. Suppose the new basis vectors are $\mathbf{e}'_j = P^i{}_j\mathbf{e}_i$ (the columns of $P$). Then:

- **Contravariant** (upper) components transform with the inverse: $v'^j = (P^{-1})^j{}_i\,v^i$. If the basis vectors double in length, the coordinates halve.
- **Covariant** (lower) components transform like the basis itself: $a'_j = P^i{}_j\,a_i$.
- A type-$(p, q)$ tensor gets one factor of $P^{-1}$ per upper index and one factor of $P$ per lower index. For a linear operator, $A' = P^{-1}AP$ (Section 7.2). For a bilinear form, $g' = P^TgP$ (previous topic).

**Einstein summation convention.** An index that appears once up and once down in the same term is summed over its range, and the summation sign is dropped:

$$w^i = A^i{}_jv^j \;\text{ means }\; w^i = \sum_j A^i{}_jv^j, \qquad a_iv^i = \sum_i a_iv^i.$$

An index that is summed is a *dummy* index and can be renamed freely. An index that is not summed is a *free* index, and it must appear on both sides of an equation. A full contraction such as $a_iv^i$ has no free indices, so it is a scalar, and the transformation factors $P$ and $P^{-1}$ cancel. That is why it is basis independent.

**Standard operations.**

| Operation | Index form | Matrix form | `einsum` |
|---|---|---|---|
| Matrix-vector product | $A^i{}_jv^j$ | $A\mathbf{v}$ | `"ij,j->i"` |
| Matrix product | $A^i{}_jB^j{}_k$ | $AB$ | `"ij,jk->ik"` |
| Trace (contraction) | $A^i{}_i$ | $\operatorname{tr}A$ | `"ii->"` |
| Outer product | $v^iw^j$ | $\mathbf{v}\mathbf{w}^T$ | `"i,j->ij"` |
| Lowering an index | $v_i = g_{ij}v^j$ | $g\mathbf{v}$ | `"ij,j->i"` |
| Bilinear form | $g_{ij}u^iv^j$ | $\mathbf{u}^Tg\mathbf{v}$ | `"ij,i,j->"` |

**Metric tensor.** An inner product is a symmetric, positive definite $(0, 2)$ tensor $g_{ij}$. It converts vectors to covectors ($v_i = g_{ij}v^j$, *lowering* an index), and its inverse $g^{ij}$ converts back (*raising* an index). In an orthonormal basis, $g_{ij} = \delta_{ij}$ and upper and lower components coincide, which is why introductory courses never distinguish them.

**Two special symbols.** The **Kronecker delta** $\delta^i{}_j$ (1 if $i = j$, else 0) is the identity tensor. The **Levi-Civita symbol** $\varepsilon_{ijk}$ is $+1$ for even permutations of $(1, 2, 3)$, $-1$ for odd ones, and $0$ if an index repeats. With it, $(\mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{w})_i = \varepsilon_{ijk}u^jw^k$ and $\det M = \varepsilon_{ijk}M_{1i}M_{2j}M_{3k}$ (Section 5.2). Here indices are all written low because the basis is orthonormal.

```python
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
A, B = rng.standard_normal((3, 4)), rng.standard_normal((4, 2))
v = rng.standard_normal(4)

# einsum is Einstein summation: repeated indices are summed, free indices remain
print(np.allclose(np.einsum("ij,jk->ik", A, B), A @ B))      # True: C^i_k = A^i_j B^j_k
print(np.allclose(np.einsum("ij,j->i", A, v), A @ v))        # True: w^i = A^i_j v^j
M = rng.standard_normal((4, 4))
print(np.isclose(np.einsum("ii->", M), np.trace(M)))         # True: contraction T^i_i

# Transformation laws. New basis vectors are the columns of P: e'_j = P^i_j e_i
P = np.array([[2.0, 1.0], [1.0, 1.0]])
v = np.array([3.0, 5.0])                      # vector components v^i (contravariant)
a = np.array([1.0, -2.0])                     # covector components a_i (covariant)
v_new = np.linalg.solve(P, v)                 # v'^j = (P^{-1})^j_i v^i
a_new = P.T @ a                               # a'_j = P^i_j a_i
print(v_new, a_new)                           # [-2.  7.] [ 0. -1.]
print(a @ v, a_new @ v_new)                   # -7.0 -7.0: the full contraction a_i v^i is invariant

# Metric tensor: raising/lowering indices. With g = I they coincide; with another g they do not
g = np.array([[2.0, 0.0], [0.0, 3.0]])        # a non-standard inner product on R^2
v_lower = g @ v                               # v_i = g_ij v^j
print(v_lower, v @ g @ v)                     # [ 6. 15.] 93.0: ||v||^2 = g_ij v^i v^j

# Levi-Civita symbol: (u x w)_i = eps_ijk u_j w_k, det(M) = eps_ijk M_1i M_2j M_3k
eps = np.zeros((3, 3, 3))
for (i, j, k), s in {(0, 1, 2): 1, (1, 2, 0): 1, (2, 0, 1): 1,
                     (0, 2, 1): -1, (2, 1, 0): -1, (1, 0, 2): -1}.items():
    eps[i, j, k] = s
u, w = np.array([1.0, 2.0, 3.0]), np.array([4.0, 5.0, 6.0])
print(np.einsum("ijk,j,k->i", eps, u, w), np.cross(u, w))   # [-3.  6. -3.] [-3.  6. -3.]
M3 = rng.standard_normal((3, 3))
print(np.isclose(np.einsum("ijk,i,j,k->", eps, M3[0], M3[1], M3[2]), np.linalg.det(M3)))  # True
```

**Key takeaways**

- A type-$(p, q)$ tensor has $p$ upper (contravariant) and $q$ lower (covariant) indices; each index fixes how components transform under a change of basis.
- Einstein convention: a repeated upper-lower index pair is summed; free indices must match on both sides of an equation.
- Full contractions (no free indices) are scalars and are invariant under change of basis.
- The metric tensor raises and lowers indices; in orthonormal coordinates the distinction disappears.
- `np.einsum` is index notation as code: products, traces, contractions, and transposes in one call.

> 2. Show that $\operatorname{tr}(A) = A^i{}_i$ is invariant under $A \mapsto P^{-1}AP$ by writing the transformed components in index form and contracting.

> 4. **Interview:** Given a batch of matrices `A` of shape `(b, n, m)` and `B` of shape `(b, m, k)`, write one `einsum` call that computes the batched products, and another that computes the trace of each product without forming it. *Hint:* keep `b` as a free index in both; for the trace, contract the outer indices as well as `m`.

#### Exterior Algebra and Wedge Products

**Why it matters.** The cross product works only in $\mathbb{R}^3$, and the determinant was introduced in Chapter 5 through formulas whose geometric meaning came later. The wedge product handles both at once, in every dimension. It measures oriented area, volume, and their higher-dimensional analogs, and it gives a definition of the determinant that makes $\det(AB) = \det A\det B$ almost automatic. It is also the algebra behind differential forms and integration on curved spaces (Section 13.4).

**Analogy.** Think of $\mathbf{u} \wedge \mathbf{w}$ as the parallelogram spanned by $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{w}$, remembered only by its area, its plane, and its orientation (a direction of circulation). Swapping the two edges reverses the orientation, and a parallelogram with two parallel edges is flat and has area zero.

**Definition.** The **wedge product** is a bilinear product that is *alternating*:

$$\mathbf{v} \wedge \mathbf{v} = 0 \quad \text{for every } \mathbf{v}.$$

Expanding $(\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{w}) \wedge (\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{w}) = 0$ gives anticommutativity, $\mathbf{u} \wedge \mathbf{w} = -\mathbf{w} \wedge \mathbf{u}$. Products of $k$ vectors span the **$k$-th exterior power** $\Lambda^kV$. If $\mathbf{e}_1, \dots, \mathbf{e}_n$ is a basis of $V$, then

$$\{\mathbf{e}_{i_1} \wedge \cdots \wedge \mathbf{e}_{i_k} : i_1 < i_2 < \cdots < i_k\} \text{ is a basis of } \Lambda^kV, \qquad \dim\Lambda^kV = \binom{n}{k}.$$

In particular $\Lambda^nV$ is one-dimensional, and $\Lambda^kV = 0$ for $k > n$.

| $k$ | $\Lambda^k\mathbb{R}^3$ basis | Dimension | Geometric meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | $1$ | 1 | scalars |
| 1 | $\mathbf{e}_1, \mathbf{e}_2, \mathbf{e}_3$ | 3 | oriented lengths (vectors) |
| 2 | $\mathbf{e}_1 \wedge \mathbf{e}_2, \mathbf{e}_1 \wedge \mathbf{e}_3, \mathbf{e}_2 \wedge \mathbf{e}_3$ | 3 | oriented areas |
| 3 | $\mathbf{e}_1 \wedge \mathbf{e}_2 \wedge \mathbf{e}_3$ | 1 | oriented volumes |

**Components are minors.** For $\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{w} \in \mathbb{R}^n$,

$$\mathbf{u} \wedge \mathbf{w} = \sum_{i < j}(u_iw_j - u_jw_i)\,\mathbf{e}_i \wedge \mathbf{e}_j.$$

Each coefficient is a $2 \times 2$ minor of the $n \times 2$ matrix $[\mathbf{u}\ \mathbf{w}]$. More generally, the coefficients of $\mathbf{v}_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge \mathbf{v}_k$ are the $k \times k$ minors of $[\mathbf{v}_1 \cdots \mathbf{v}_k]$. In $\mathbb{R}^3$, the three components of $\mathbf{u} \wedge \mathbf{w}$ are, up to order and sign, the components of $\mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{w}$. The cross product is the wedge product, converted back into a vector by the normal direction. That conversion (the *Hodge star*) only produces a vector when $n = 3$, which is why the cross product exists only in three dimensions.

**The determinant, intrinsically.** In top degree,

$$\mathbf{v}_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge \mathbf{v}_n = \det[\mathbf{v}_1 \cdots \mathbf{v}_n]\;\mathbf{e}_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge \mathbf{e}_n.$$

A linear map $T : V \to V$ induces $\Lambda^nT$ on the one-dimensional space $\Lambda^nV$, via $\mathbf{v}_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge \mathbf{v}_n \mapsto T\mathbf{v}_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge T\mathbf{v}_n$. Any linear map on a one-dimensional space is multiplication by a scalar, and that scalar is $\det T$. This definition needs no basis. It also proves the product rule in one line: $\Lambda^n(ST) = \Lambda^nS \circ \Lambda^nT$, so $\det(ST) = \det S\,\det T$.

**Main facts.**

- *Independence test:* $\mathbf{v}_1, \dots, \mathbf{v}_k$ are linearly independent if and only if $\mathbf{v}_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge \mathbf{v}_k \ne 0$.
- *Subspaces:* if $\{\mathbf{v}_i\}$ and $\{\mathbf{w}_i\}$ span the same $k$-dimensional subspace, their wedges differ only by a nonzero scalar (the determinant of the change of basis). The minors therefore encode the subspace itself; they are its *Plücker coordinates*.
- *Volume:* the $k$-dimensional volume of the parallelotope spanned by $\mathbf{v}_1, \dots, \mathbf{v}_k$ is the Euclidean length of the coefficient vector. By the Cauchy-Binet formula, its square equals the Gram determinant $\det(V^TV)$.

```python
import numpy as np
from itertools import combinations

def wedge(*vectors):
    """Components of v1 ^ ... ^ vk in the basis e_I, I = (i1 < ... < ik): the k x k minors."""
    V = np.column_stack(vectors)              # n x k
    n, k = V.shape
    return {I: np.linalg.det(V[list(I), :]) for I in combinations(range(n), k)}

u = np.array([1.0, 2.0, 3.0])
w = np.array([4.0, 5.0, 6.0])
print({I: float(round(c, 6)) for I, c in wedge(u, w).items()})
# {(0, 1): -3.0, (0, 2): -6.0, (1, 2): -3.0}     coefficients of e1^e2, e1^e3, e2^e3
print(np.cross(u, w))                         # [-3.  6. -3.]: the same numbers, reordered as
                                              # (e2^e3, e3^e1, e1^e2) = (-3, -(-6), -3)

# Antisymmetry: w ^ u = -(u ^ w), and u ^ u = 0
print(all(np.isclose(wedge(w, u)[I], -c) for I, c in wedge(u, w).items()))   # True
print(max(abs(c) for c in wedge(u, u).values()))                          # 0.0

# Independence test: v1 ^ ... ^ vk != 0  iff  the vectors are independent
x = u + 2 * w                                 # dependent on u, w
print(max(abs(c) for c in wedge(u, w, x).values()))                       # 0.0

# Top degree: v1 ^ v2 ^ v3 = det[v1 v2 v3] e1^e2^e3
z = np.array([0.0, 1.0, 1.0])
print({I: float(round(c, 6)) for I, c in wedge(u, w, z).items()})          # {(0, 1, 2): 3.0}
print(round(np.linalg.det(np.column_stack([u, w, z])), 6))                # 3.0

# Squared k-volume = sum of squared minors = Gram determinant (Cauchy-Binet)
G = np.column_stack([u, w]).T @ np.column_stack([u, w])
print(sum(c**2 for c in wedge(u, w).values()), round(np.linalg.det(G), 6))   # 54.0 54.0: area = sqrt(54)
```

**Key takeaways**

- The wedge product is bilinear and alternating: $\mathbf{v} \wedge \mathbf{v} = 0$ and $\mathbf{u} \wedge \mathbf{w} = -\mathbf{w} \wedge \mathbf{u}$.
- $\Lambda^kV$ has dimension $\binom{n}{k}$; the components of $\mathbf{v}_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge \mathbf{v}_k$ are the $k \times k$ minors of $[\mathbf{v}_1 \cdots \mathbf{v}_k]$.
- A wedge product is nonzero exactly when its factors are independent; its length is the $k$-volume they span.
- In top degree, $\Lambda^nT$ is multiplication by $\det T$: a basis-free definition of the determinant that makes the product rule immediate.
- The cross product is the $n = 3$ special case of $\mathbf{u} \wedge \mathbf{w}$, turned into a vector.

> 🧪 Practice

> 2. Compute the area of the parallelogram in $\mathbb{R}^4$ spanned by $(1, 0, 1, 0)$ and $(0, 1, 1, 1)$ in two ways: from the six $2 \times 2$ minors, and from the Gram determinant.
